/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
import re,statistics
text=Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').read_text()
sec=text.split('=== PAGE 13 ===')[1].split('=== PAGE 14 ===')[0]
rows=[]
for l in sec.splitlines():
 m=re.match(r'\\s*(.*?)\\s+(-?\\d+\\.\\d+)\\s+(\\d+\\.\\d+)\\s+(-?\\d+\\.\\d+)\\s+(\\d+\\.\\d+)\\s+(.*)',l)
 if m: rows.append((m.group(1),*[float(m.group(i)) for i in range(2,6)],m.group(6)))
print('Occupation rows:',len(rows))
for label,rr in [('All',rows),('Male-stereotyped',rows[:20]),('Female-stereotyped',rows[20:])]:
 print(label,'mean STS single, paired:',*[round(statistics.mean(r[i] for r in rr),4) for i in [1,3]],'mean %F single, paired:',*[round(statistics.mean(r[i] for r in rr),4) for i in [2,4]])
print('Descriptive mean absolute micro STS single, paired:',*[round(statistics.mean(abs(r[i]) for r in rows),4) for i in [1,3]])
sec=text.split('=== PAGE 15 ===')[1]
rows=[]
for l in sec.splitlines():
 m=re.match(r'\\s*(.*?)\\s+(minor|power)\\s+(-?\\d+\\.\\d+)\\s+(-?\\d+\\.\\d+)\\s+(-?\\d+\\.\\d+)',l)
 if m: rows.append((m.group(1),m.group(2),*[float(m.group(i)) for i in range(3,6)]))
print('Power rows:',len(rows))
for label,rr in [('All',rows),('Powerful',[r for r in rows if r[1]=='power']),('Powerless',[r for r in rows if r[1]=='minor'])]:
 print(label,'mean single, paired, gap:',*[round(statistics.mean(r[i] for r in rr),4) for i in [2,3,4]])
PY"

strengths: PST addresses a relevant gap in multimodal NLP evaluation: gender associations can change when multiple people and social roles appear together. The occupational results provide useful evidence of this contextual effect.

The occupational experiment systematically covers 400 occupation pairs in both orders, producing 800 images. Three human annotators and high reported agreement (Fleiss’ kappa 0.88–0.92) support the reliability of the appearance labels.

The manuscript clearly presents the evaluation idea and supplies occupation lists, prompt templates, annotation instructions, and detailed results. Testing BLIP against human annotations usefully demonstrates why automated labeling would be unreliable here.
weaknesses: STS measures signed stereotype conformity, not the stated absolute level of gender bias. Opposing scores cancel: Table 3 averages +50 for female-stereotyped occupations and −30 for male-stereotyped occupations into 10, despite feminine-skewed outputs in both groups. The results support increased stereotype conformity under PST, but do not establish that single-person generation is fair or that pairing increases absolute gender imbalance. A complementary parity measure and more precise claims are needed.

The organizational-power comparison is not demonstrably controlled for descriptor wording. In Figure 6, the developer example uses 'leader' and 'employee' individually but 'manager' and 'assistant' when paired. Table 16 reports only generic power categories, obscuring the actual assignments. Matched descriptors are necessary to distinguish the effect of pairing from lexical differences.

Only three single-person images are sampled per identity, versus 40 paired appearances per occupation. This makes occupation-level rankings and extreme anti-stereotype examples uncertain. Reversing prompt order is a useful control, but does not establish statistical significance; confidence intervals or suitable statistical analyses are missing.

Reproducibility and annotation validity remain incomplete. The manuscript does not document the DALL-E 3 access interface, generation dates/settings, treatment of prompt rewriting, or provide an image/label archive or analysis-code link. It also omits label aggregation and handling of 'Cannot Identify' responses. Agreement about perceived gender does not establish that the requested roles appeared on the intended sides; instruction-following failures need an explicit audit.

Evidence is limited to one model and one main prompt template, while occupational mitigation is evaluated only on selected highly biased occupations. These support a focused exploratory contribution, but leave robustness and mitigation effectiveness uncertain. The useful occupational finding makes Findings plausible; unresolved measurement, comparison, and reproducibility concerns prevent a clear positive recommendation.
